query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing local chemical order via controlled annealing increases electron coherence and strengthens electron–phonon coupling in the HEA, leading to a higher superconducting Tc and a sharper transition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast high-entropy alloy with full chemical disorder and a pseudocrystalline bcc lattice.
generation.intervention: Apply an annealing treatment (varying temperature and time) designed to partially relieve local chemical disorder while maintaining the overall composition and crystal phase.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature regime (below ~10 K) at ambient pressure, ensuring no phase transformation occurs during annealing.
generation.mechanism: The annealing process promotes short-range ordering without altering the global bcc lattice. This local ordering enhances electron coherence and optimizes electron–phonon interactions, which in turn facilitates stronger Cooper pairing and a more uniform superconducting phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-cast state, the annealed HEA should exhibit a noticeable increase in Tc and a sharper superconducting transition (evidenced by a steeper drop in resistance and a more defined specific heat discontinuity).
generation.baseline: The baseline is the as-cast, fully disordered HEA, which is expected to have a lower Tc and a broader (smeared) superconducting transition due to heterogeneous local environments.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold under low-temperature conditions (below approximately 10 K) and when annealing is controlled to modify local order without triggering phase segregation or bulk phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the Tc increase and the degree of transition sharpening are not precisely determined and may show modest changes; further experimental characterization is necessary to quantify these shifts.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and characterize two sets of HEA samples: one kept in the as-cast state and another subjected to a controlled annealing treatment to enhance local chemical order. Perform low-temperature measurements (electrical resistance, specific heat, and magnetic susceptibility) on both sets.
measurements: Critical temperature (Tc) from resistance and susceptibility data
Transition sharpness (width of superconducting transition in resistance and specific heat jump)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in Tc or a sharper superconducting transition compared to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis that local chemical ordering enhances superconductivity in this HEA is falsified.

A sharp drop to a zero-resistance superconducting state is observed at ∼7.7 K (we define TC as the temperature where the resistance changes from a finite value to zero), consistent with the results reported in ref. . Applying a magnetic field on the sample shows that its superconducting transition temperature (TC) systematically shifts to lower temperature (Fig. 1A, Inset), as expected. Temperature-dependent constant-current magnetic susceptibility characterization was also performed for the ambient-pressure sample. As shown in Fig. 1B, a strong diamagnetic response is observed starting at 7.6 K, indicative of a bulk superconducting nature. High-pressure resistance measurements were performed for four samples that were cut from the material used as the standard for the superconductivity at ambient pressure. The electrical resistance measurements for these samples were performed between 4 and 300 K. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. It has long been recognized that a critical amount of disorder can suppress superconductivity near the Anderson quantum phase transition. The observed Tc reduction concomitant with a mixing entropy ΔS enhancement in superconducting HEAs seems to agree with that picture. On the other hand, recent analyses of competing interaction-channels in strongly disordered metals predict a Tc enhancement within the BCS framework, when the electron system is tuned to a quantum critical point,. This hypothesis finds support in a recent study of HEA (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x thin films; while each of the binary alloys TaNb and HfZrTi does not show a superconducting transition at or above 2 K, all solid solutions of (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x at various mixing ratios x are superconducting at Tc≤6.9 K. This ’cocktail’ effect suggests an intricate relation between the presence of strong compositional disorder, realized through the random arrangement of five atomic species on a bcc lattice, and superconductivity, which is an interesting question to address experimentally.

We have experimentally studied the superconducting state of the HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x In thin film form with x=0.35 and x=0.71 by measuring Hc1(T) and Hc2(T). Our analysis of λ(T) is in quantitative agreement with the BCS theory of an isotropic single band s-wave superconductor in the weak coupling limit. The analysis of ξ(T) reveals a comparable amount of disorder at both compositions, lx=0.35≈lx=0.71. Therefore, we can exclude that the observed variations in Tc originate from a disorder-driven mechanism. Further theoretical and experimental studies will be needed to characterize the low-energy electronic structure at various alloy compositions and its influence on Tc. Looking ahead, results of such efforts may inform pathways for realizing HEAs with enhanced superconducting Tc. Employing penetration-depth measurements to other superconducting HEAs, such as those crystallizing on the CsCl-type lattice, it will be interesting to test whether weak coupling s-wave superconductivity is a common occurrence in these material systems. frame.system: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a multi-element, disordered crystal structure in its as-cast, uncharacterized state.
frame.goal: To determine the mechanistic origin of superconductivity in the HEA at low temperatures, specifically how electronic interactions (e.g., electron–phonon coupling or unconventional pairing interactions due to chemical disorder) lead to the emergence of superconductivity.
frame.limitation: The superconducting behavior of the HEA is entirely uncharacterized with unknown critical temperatures, pairing mechanisms, or the influence of chemical disorder on electron coherence.

decision.trend: Early work on HEA superconductors (PMC5740615) established that robust zero-resistance superconductivity can exist under extreme pressures, hinting that disorder inherent in these alloys does not necessarily preclude coherent electron pairing. Subsequent studies (PMC9098454) expanded on this by showing that the superconducting state in HEA-type tellurides is unusually robust under external pressure, suggesting a link between configurational entropy and superconducting behavior. Later, investigations (PMC9329343) provided detailed characterization of the superconducting order parameter in HEAs, supporting a conventional isotropic s‑wave, BCS-like scenario despite high compositional disorder. Most recently (PMC10489023), critical superconducting parameters such as Tc and upper critical fields were measured in a new Nb–Ti–Zr–Ta–Hf HEA, reinforcing the observation of conventional electron–phonon coupling mechanisms while raising questions about the role of local chemical disorder in tuning these parameters.
decision.unsolved: While the overall superconducting state appears conventional, it remains unclear how the high level of chemical disorder in HEAs (and potential local fluctuations in atomic order) specifically governs the electron–phonon coupling—which in turn determines Tc, pairing strength, and coherence—even in the absence of structural phase transitions. In particular, a controlled baseline comparison between the as-cast, fully disordered state and a state with modulated local ordering is lacking, which would elucidate whether enhanced local order strengthens electron coherence and modifies superconducting properties within a defined temperature (and possibly pressure) range.
decision.lever: Introduce and control the degree of local chemical order via annealing treatments (varying temperature/time) to partially relieve the inherent chemical disorder while keeping the global phase and composition unchanged
decision.why: Based on the trend, prior studies have characterized the superconducting state in fully disordered HEAs and established that superconductivity is robust even under high pressures; however, the mechanistic role of local chemical order remains unexplored. A controlled variable experiment comparing the baseline (as-cast state) to samples with systematically increased local order will directly test the hypothesis that local ordering modulates electron–phonon coupling. Expected observations include shifts in Tc, modifications of the superconducting gap, or changes in the transition sharpness over a low-temperature range. A clear falsification criterion would be if no significant difference in superconducting parameters is observed between the as-cast and annealed states, indicating that local chemical ordering does not govern the superconducting mechanism in these HEAs.
